name: Finding the Minimum Value in a List
description: Write a program that finds the minimum value in a list.
code:
#Step 1: Define and initialize the list
values = [5, 8, 4, 78, 95, 12, 1, 0, 6, 35, 46]
#Step 2: Set the first value to be the minimum value so far.
min_value = values[0]
#Step 3: Iterate through the remaining values in the list and decide which one is the minimum value 
for i in range(1, len(values)): 
    # Step 3.1: Determine if the element at index i is the minimum value so far
    if (values[i] < min_value):
        min_value = values[i]
#Step 4: Print the minimum value in the list
print("Minimum value:", min_value)

commentList: You create a variable named values and assign it a list of integers; this list is the data your program will search to find the minimum value.
You use the '=' operator to bind a list literal to the name values. The square brackets [...] define a list and elements are comma-separated, so values becomes an indexable, iterable list object.
You should be aware that accessing values[0] later will fail with an IndexError if the list is empty — this literal has items, but in general you should check for an empty list before indexing.

Watch for common mistakes: forgetting commas between elements is a syntax error, mixing incompatible types (e.g., ints and strings) can cause TypeError when you compare elements, and a typo in the name values later will raise a NameError.

Best practices: use a clear variable name, avoid hard-coding data in production (read input or load from a file), consider using Python's built-in min(values) for simplicity, and explicitly handle the empty-list case before using values[0].

commentList: You set min_value to the first element of values so you have a starting baseline to compare every other element against when searching for the smallest number.
This uses indexing: values[0] accesses the element at index 0 (the first item in the list) and the = operator assigns that value to the variable min_value.
If values is empty, values[0] will raise an IndexError, so you should check the list is not empty before this line (for example: if not values: handle the empty case).
A common misconception is that min_value remains linked to the list item; for immutable types like integers, min_value is a separate value, so changing min_value does not modify values[0].

Best practice: keep a clear name like min_value (don’t name the variable min because that would shadow Python’s built-in min() function), and consider alternatives like using min(values) or iterating with for v in values[1:] to make your intent clearer.

commentList: You use this line to loop over every index from 1 up to the last index of values so you can compare each remaining element to min_value.

You can read the syntax as: 'for' starts a loop, 'i' is the loop variable (an index), range(1, len(values)) produces the integers 1, 2, ..., len(values)-1, and the trailing colon begins the indented loop body where you access elements with values[i].

You must be careful about off-by-one and empty-list errors: range(1, len(values)) correctly excludes len(values) (so the last index is len(values)-1), but using range(1, len(values)+1) would cause an IndexError; also the code earlier uses values[0], so you should check for an empty list before this loop to avoid an exception.

You could iterate over elements directly for clearer code, e.g. for v in values[1:]: if v < min_value: min_value = v, or use Python's built-in min(values) for a concise solution. Also prefer descriptive names (like idx or index) instead of i to improve readability.

You should ensure proper indentation after the colon and avoid changing the list while iterating; the loop variable i is reused each iteration (which is normal), and you should not reinitialize min_value inside the loop.

commentList: You use this line to test whether the current list element (values[i]) is smaller than the smallest value you've seen so far (min_value); the following indented block runs only when that test is true.

You can read the syntax as: 'if' starts a conditional, '(values[i] < min_value)' is the comparison that returns True or False, and the trailing ':' begins the code block that runs when the condition is True. The parentheses are optional in Python.
You must keep this line indented exactly under the for-loop so it runs once per element. values[i] refers to the element at index i from the loop (so this check happens for each remaining element).

Be careful not to use '=' here — that would try to assign instead of compare. Also note that if the list were empty you'd already get an error before this line because values[0] was used to initialize min_value; always check for an empty list first if that can happen.

A small improvement you might use: iterate directly with 'for val in values[1:]:' and then write 'if val < min_value:' — it makes the code clearer. Or, when appropriate, use Python's built-in min(values) for a shorter solution.

commentList: This line updates the running minimum: when the current element values[i] is smaller than min_value, you assign that element to min_value so the program remembers the new smallest value.

Syntactically, '=' is the assignment operator that stores the right-hand expression (values[i]) into the variable on the left (min_value). values[i] accesses the list element at index i, and because this line is indented inside the if-block it only runs when the condition is true.

A common misconception is to think this changes the list — it doesn't; you only change the variable min_value, not the contents of values. Also note this approach assumes the list is not empty (values[0] would have already failed if it were) and that all elements are comparable (mixing types like numbers and strings can raise a TypeError).

Watch your indentation: the line must be indented under the if statement so it executes only when the condition is met. Wrong indentation can make the program behave incorrectly or raise an IndentationError.

Best practices: check for an empty list before starting the loop, keep a clear variable name (min_value avoids shadowing the built-in min), and consider using the built-in min(values) or iterating with for value in values[1:] for clearer, more Pythonic code.

commentList: Purpose: This line prints the result so the user can see it. You are showing the label "Minimum value:" followed by the value stored in min_value, which was computed earlier by the loop.

Syntax and semantics: print("Minimum value:", min_value) calls Python's print function with two arguments separated by a comma. Python converts min_value to a string for display and inserts a space between the arguments. In Python 3 the parentheses are required.

Potential errors and misconceptions: If min_value was never defined (for example, because the list was empty and the code failed at values[0]), this line would raise a NameError. Also be aware that print only displays the value—it does not return it for further computation.

Best practices: Before printing, you should check for an empty list and handle that case (e.g., print a message or raise an error). For clearer formatting you can use an f-string: print(f"Minimum value: {min_value}"). For real programs consider returning the value from a function or using Python's built-in min(values) when appropriate.

distractors.description: Why you might pick this: you may accidentally flip the comparison sign because you are thinking in terms of finding a 'different' value or you confuse 'smaller than' with 'greater than'. This is a very common sign error. What happens if you use it: the code will update min_value whenever it finds a value that is larger than the current min_value. As the loop runs, min_value will be replaced by progressively larger elements and you will end up with the largest number in the list instead of the smallest. How this goes wrong for the program: instead of checking for values that are smaller and choosing those, this line chooses bigger values — so the variable ends up holding the maximum. In short, the comparison direction is wrong: you're selecting the wrong side of the relation, so the algorithm no longer finds a minimum.

Step-by-step: you might pick this because you see i changing each loop and think it represents the current element. If you use this line, you store the index number (like 1, 2, 3) into the variable that is supposed to track the smallest element. As a result, when you print the result you get a position from the list, not the actual smallest element. The program will not crash, but the output will be the wrong quantity and the rest of the comparisons will compare values to an index instead of to a real list element. This is wrong because you are replacing the thing you should be tracking (the element itself) with the loop position — the roles are swapped and the intended minimum value is never recorded correctly.

Step-by-step: you might pick this because you think the list itself should be changed to reflect the minimum found so far. Using this line will overwrite the current list element with whatever value you had stored as the minimum, instead of updating the variable that holds the minimum. That modifies the original data and does not update the tracked minimum value. The program may continue to run but will produce incorrect results and will corrupt the list contents. This is incorrect because it updates the wrong place — you alter the list instead of changing the variable that should record the new minimum.
